name: Maxingshigan-yinqiaosan (Chinese herbal decoction)
short: Contains ephedra: ephedra weight-loss supplements (not this decoction) linked to stroke, deaths; 1 liver failure with ma huang. One open H1N1 trial: 2 given the decoction reported nausea and vomiting.
text: Herbs: the trial abstract describes maxingshigan-yinqiaosan as a decoction of 12 Chinese herbal medicines, including honey-fried ephedra (Herba Ephedrae); it does not list the other 11. Trial: in a non-blinded randomized trial at 11 Chinese hospitals, 410 people aged 15 to 69 with laboratory-confirmed H1N1 influenza received oseltamivir, the decoction, both, or no treatment for 5 days; two patients who received the decoction reported nausea and vomiting. The abstract does not say how many people took the decoction, how adverse events were collected, or whether any other events occurred, and the authors note that participants were young and had mild infection. Ephedra: a review of Kampo medicines in general (Japanese formulas; the abstract does not name this decoction) lists sympathomimetic symptoms caused by ephedra among adverse effects linked to overdose. Ephedra supplements and ephedrine (the abstracts do not name this decoction): a review of 140 reports to the US Food and Drug Administration about dietary supplements containing ephedra alkaloids, promoted for weight loss and energy, judged 31% definitely or probably related to the supplements; hypertension, palpitations or fast heart rate, stroke and seizures were reported, ten events resulted in death and 13 in permanent disability; and a meta-analysis of safety data from 50 trials of ephedra or ephedrine for weight loss or athletic performance found 2.2- to 3.6-fold higher odds of psychiatric, autonomic or gastrointestinal symptoms and heart palpitations. Other ephedra data (the abstract does not name this decoction): a later meta-analysis of 16 randomized trials of ephedra-containing oral medications for weight reduction found no significant difference in adverse effects between treatment and control groups; the authors note that ephedra is widely used in forms including food supplements and herbal prescriptions, and the abstract does not say which products the trials tested. Kidneys (ephedrine and ephedra; neither abstract names this decoction): a case report describes ephedrine kidney stones in a person using a ma-huang energy supplement, and the authors state that a kidney-stone database shows this is an endemic complication of ephedrine, with hundreds of previous episodes; a review of nephrotoxicity of Chinese herbal medicines, which had no limit on research type, names Ephedra sinica among six Chinese herbal medicines with a risk of nephrotoxicity that had a large number of studies (two studies for Ephedra sinica); the abstract does not describe the harms or say whether those studies were in people. Ephedra and the liver (case reports; neither abstract names this decoction): one case report describes fulminant liver failure needing a liver transplant associated with ma huang, which the authors describe as a traditional Chinese remedy containing ephedrine-type alkaloids; the abstract does not say what product was taken or why, or give the patient's age or sex. Another describes acute hepatitis with a ma-huang herbal product advertised for weight loss and energy, which the authors speculate contained another ingredient or contaminant or was misidentified. PubMed searches found no other study reporting adverse events with this decoction, and no report of liver injury, kidney injury or heavy-metal contamination naming it. No interaction data were found in the cited sources; the trial gave the decoction with oseltamivir in one group, and its abstract reports no interaction.
